question: What is the main focus of cancer epidemiology?

options.A: Testing new chemotherapy drugs in the laboratory
options.B: Studying cancer patterns and causes in populations
options.C: Performing surgical removal of malignant tumors
options.D: Providing daily bedside care to cancer patients

explanation: Cancer epidemiology looks at whole groups of people to see how and why cancer occurs in different populations. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why do public health planners rely on epidemiological data?

options.A: To decide where to direct health resources and programs
options.B: To diagnose individual patients in emergency rooms
options.C: To write personal care plans for recovering clients
options.D: To determine the exact cost of hospital equipment

explanation: Population data helps health authorities see where disease rates are highest so they can build facilities and plan interventions accordingly. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which cancer is the most common among Nigerian women?
explanation: Breast cancer is recorded as the leading malignancy among women in Nigeria and globally. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is a major viral infection linked closely to cervical cancer in Nigeria?
explanation: Persistent infection with high-risk strains of Human Papillomavirus is the primary driver behind most cervical cancer cases. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What does incidence measure in a population?

options.A: The number of new cases diagnosed
options.B: The total number of existing cases
options.C: The percentage of people who die
options.D: The cost of treating the disease

explanation: Incidence specifically counts the new diagnoses appearing over a set timeframe, showing the rate at which a disease develops. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: A public health nurse wants to know the total burden of chronic leukemia in a community, including people diagnosed years ago. Which measure should she look at?
explanation: Prevalence measures all existing cases at a given time, capturing both new diagnoses and survivors living with the condition. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following is a non-modifiable risk factor for cancer?
explanation: Age is an inherent biological factor that cannot be altered, making it non-modifiable. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why are infectious agents like Hepatitis B classified as cancer risk factors?

options.A: They immediately destroy all red blood cells in the body
options.B: They lower body temperature and stop normal digestion
options.C: They block the absorption of vital nutrients in the gut
options.D: They cause chronic inflammation and cellular damage over time

explanation: Certain viruses and bacteria lead to long-term tissue damage and inflammation, which increases the chance of cellular mutations. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the origin of most cancer-causing mutations?

options.A: Passed down exclusively through maternal bloodlines
options.B: Inherited directly from parents in every single diagnosed case
options.C: Acquired over a lifetime from environmental and lifestyle factors
options.D: Caused entirely by sudden bacterial infections in childhood

explanation: Most cancers arise from acquired mutations that build up over time due to exposure to external agents like tobacco, radiation, and unhealthy diets. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why do people with the same genetic background sometimes have different cancer risks?

options.A: Genetics is the only factor that ever influences disease
options.B: Inherited genes change completely every five years
options.C: Their environmental exposures and lifestyle choices vary
options.D: Lifestyle habits have no real impact on cellular health

explanation: Environmental and lifestyle factors interact with genes, meaning different habits will alter overall risk even among family members. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of cancer screening programs?

options.A: To replace traditional biopsy procedures entirely
options.B: To detect cancer or precancerous changes early
options.C: To cure late-stage metastatic disease completely
options.D: To measure the exact cost of hospital stays

explanation: Screening aims to identify disease before symptoms appear so treatment can start when it is most effective. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: A community health nurse is planning a cervical cancer screening outreach. Which test is she most likely to utilize?
explanation: A Pap smear is a standard, widely used screening tool for detecting cervical cell abnormalities and precancerous lesions. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h6)

question: How do nurses directly help with cancer epidemiology in clinical and community settings?

options.A: Funding public health research grants through private banks
options.B: Designing blueprints for modern oncology radiation bunkers
options.C: Manufacturing new chemotherapy drugs in hospital pharmacies
options.D: Accurate data collection and maintaining cancer registries

explanation: Nurses play a huge role by gathering precise patient data and keeping records updated, which helps researchers track cancer trends. You're making great progress! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)

question: Why are community health nurses in a great position to promote cancer prevention?

options.A: They are the only healthcare professionals permitted to diagnose tumors
options.B: They hold exclusive authority over national public health budgets
options.C: They interact directly with individuals and families on a regular basis
options.D: They spend all their time working inside high-tech molecular laboratories

explanation: Because nurses interact regularly with everyday people and families, they are perfectly placed to teach about risk factors and encourage healthy habits. Well done! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h7)
